name: french potato lentils
instructions:
A french/italian lentil + mushroom + potato stew. Built on pureed portabella mushrooms + finely chopped potatoes + lentils; the three of them fill the 'meat' slot together (see notes). CURRENT OPTIMAL BUILD: a small amount of tomato paste + a lot of stock, plus butter + flour + dijon mustard for enrichment. Details below.

=== PROCEDURE ===

1. SOFFRITO IN BUTTER + OLIVE OIL: sauté finely chopped yellow onion, celery, and carrots in butter + olive oil until softened. Butter is a real part of the flavor now — see enrichment note.
2. PUREED PORTABELLAS: puree the portabella mushrooms in a food processor or blender, then add to the pot. Cook them down into the soffrito base — they should reduce and deepen in color.
3. TOMATO PASTE — SMALL AMOUNT, COOKED HARD: add a small spoonful of tomato paste (not a lot) and cook it hard into the oil until it darkens a shade. A little bit here goes a long way — see optimal-build note.
4. FLOUR — LIGHT ROUX: dust all-purpose flour onto the vegetables + mushrooms and stir briefly to coat, giving a light roux before liquid goes in. See enrichment note.
5. HERBS + SEASONING: add bay leaf and rosemary (mix of both, not just rosemary — see herbs note). Herbes de provence and/or oregano welcome too. Season with black pepper and salt.
6. POTATOES + LENTILS: fold in finely chopped potatoes (small dice — see notes) and lentils. Both go in at the same time so they cook at the same rate.
7. LOTS OF STOCK: pour in a generous amount of stock — this is the primary broth medium. Less tomato + more stock is the current optimal, see notes.
8. SLOW COOK covered for a long time.
9. DIJON MUSTARD + CREAM — STIR IN NEAR THE END: stir in a spoonful of dijon mustard and a splash of heavy cream toward the end of the cook. Both should be SILENT in the finished stew — the lentil + potato starch absorbs them into the body (see THE LOGIC OF THE DISH). This is the load-bearing enrichment — see mustard-and-mushroom pairing note.
10. STARCH SLURRY FINISH (OPTIONAL): the butter + flour roux and the potatoes usually carry enough body, but if the broth still reads thin, stir in a small starch slurry at the end.
notes:
=== THE LOGIC OF THE DISH — ITALIAN LENTILS, RESCUED FRENCH ===

The dish builds off ITALIAN LENTILS — a soffrito of vegetables + tomato + lentils — but with the tomato pulled back: a mix of stock and tomato paste, leaning on the stock/bouillon side as much as possible. That stock-lean base alone is NOT a very interesting stew. It needs help, and each addition has a specific job:

- POTATOES: add a sweetness and savoriness you don't normally get in the minestrone stack. They're not filler — they're the flavor dimension the stock-lean base is missing.
- MUSTARD + CREAM: do a ton of the heavy lifting. Done carefully you don't even TASTE them — the starch load from the lentils and potatoes absorbs them into the body of the stew. They're silent balancers (same silent-ingredient logic as [[spinach-ricotta]]'s miso/nooch rule): they round and enrich without announcing themselves.
- PUREED MUSHROOMS: mostly there to BALANCE/TAME THE TOMATO — the same job they do in the anglo-german side of this pair ([[milk-stout-cottage-lentils]]). Body is a side benefit; tomato moderation is the assignment.
- WHITE WINE: secondary, but it works (see the wine note below).

In short: italian skeleton, tomato demoted, and a french enrichment kit (potato sweetness + silent mustard/cream + mushroom-tamed tomato) doing the work the tomato used to do.

=== NAMED 'FRENCH POTATO LENTILS' — THE CONTRAST-PAIR NAME ===

Named as one half of the lentil contrast pair with [[milk-stout-cottage-lentils]]: each name carries the register's defining ingredient (POTATO here, MILK STOUT there) plus the lentils. The name commits the recipe to the FRENCH register — the wine/cream/mustard balancer kit's home.

MUSHROOM ISN'T IN THE NAME BUT IS STILL LOAD-BEARING: the pureed portabella base is as structural as ever (see the pureed-mushrooms notes below) — it just lost the naming slot to the contrast-pair scheme. Earlier names ('lentil mushroom stew', 'lentil potato stew', 'lentil mushroom potato stew') cycled through emphasis debates; the current name settles it by naming the REGISTER MARKER rather than trying to list every load-bearing component.

=== WHY THIS BASE WORKS — POTATOES + PUREED MUSHROOMS ARE THE 'MEAT' ===

The pureed mushrooms + finely chopped potatoes fill the 'meat' slot together. In a bolognese or lentil chili, the meat is the meat; here, the mushroom-and-potato combo carries the protein-and-body role. The base itself is cuisine-neutral and historically took seasonings from either french or italian directions — but the recipe has since COMMITTED FRENCH (the wine/cream/mustard balancer kit, the contrast-pair naming vs [[milk-stout-cottage-lentils]]). The italian direction lives on only as optional seasoning leans (oregano, fennel — see herbs note). This is what distinguishes french potato lentils from italian minestrone (committed to the italian tomato path) and from french-chicken-soup (committed to the wine-and-herb broth path).

=== OPTIMAL BUILD — SMALL TOMATO PASTE + LOTS OF STOCK ===

The recipe has a tomato-vs-stock variation axis, but the current optimal build sits on the stock-forward end: a SMALL amount of tomato paste (cooked hard into the oil) + LOTS OF STOCK. Not no-tomato-paste (the paste's darkened concentration does real work in the depth-and-color slot), but not tomato-heavy either. The stock is the primary broth medium; the paste is a background savory buttress.

The fully tomato-forward direction (1-2 whole chopped tomatoes + a spoonful of paste + minimum stock) is still valid — reads dense and italian-ragu-adjacent — but the current preferred build leans stock-forward. Whole fresh tomato can be skipped entirely in the stock-forward build; the paste is enough tomato.

LESS TOMATO PASTE THAN THE ENGLISH VERSION — COUNTERINTUITIVE BUT TRUE: this recipe needs LESS tomato paste than [[milk-stout-cottage-lentils]] does, even though the english one comes out DARKER in color (the marmite/beer darkening). The reason: the french ingredients (wine, cream, mustard, potato) MESH with tomato rather than fight it — a little paste integrates and spreads through the whole base, so a little is enough. The english build's bitter ingredients (stout, marmite) push against the tomato, so it takes MORE paste to hold the warmth leg of the structure — the color just doesn't show it because the mushroom + dark beer block the red. Don't calibrate tomato paste by color; calibrate by register.

=== POTATOES ARE NON-OPTIONAL — FINELY CHOPPED, ADDED WITH THE LENTILS ===

Potatoes are load-bearing, not an optional add-on. Chop them FINELY (small dice — not large chunks) so they cook at roughly the same rate as the lentils, and add them at the same time. The potatoes contribute two things the dish needs: (1) starchy body that thickens the broth structurally as it simmers, replacing much of the need for the starch slurry finish, and (2) a starchy carb texture in each bite that softens the otherwise-monolithic lentil-and-mushroom mouthfeel. Without potatoes the stew reads thin and one-textured. Finely chopping — not chunk-cutting — matters because you want the potato distributed through every spoonful.

=== PUREED MUSHROOMS — NOT CHOPPED ===

Portabella mushrooms should be pureed (food processor or blender) before adding, then cooked down into the base. Pureeing gives them a dense meaty backbone that reads as protein-and-body rather than as visible mushroom pieces. This matches the potato-as-carb move — both structural ingredients dissolve into the broth and support it structurally rather than showing up as discrete chunks. Chopped mushrooms give you a different (chunkier, less integrated) dish.

PUREED MUSHROOMS ALSO MODERATE THE TOMATO (CROSS-RECIPE LESSON): the mushroom paste darkens and grounds the base so the tomato paste can do its depth work WITHOUT turning the dish red/tomato-forward or running the show. Confirmed in both this stew and [[milk-stout-cottage-lentils]]'s dark build (where pureed mushrooms + dark beer produced a properly dark broth despite real tomato paste in the pot). If a lentil dish wants tomato's depth but not tomato's dominance, the pureed-mushroom base is the mechanism.

=== HERBS — BAY LEAF + ROSEMARY IS OPTIMAL (TOO MUCH ROSEMARY ALONE IS BAD) ===

The current optimal herb mix is bay leaf + rosemary together. Bay leaf sits quietly in the simmer adding depth without pushing a direction; rosemary provides the piney second dimension against the mushroom-and-lentil base. Together they hit the right herb balance for this stew.

ROSEMARY ALONE (WITHOUT BAY LEAF) IS EASY TO OVERDO: rosemary at full quantity dominates the dish. Bay leaf's quiet background presence absorbs some of what rosemary is trying to do and prevents rosemary from taking over. Use rosemary lightly even in the mix; use bay leaf freely.

HERBES DE PROVENCE AND DRIED OREGANO ARE FINE ADDITIONS BUT NOT REQUIRED: both work alongside bay leaf + rosemary if you want more herb complexity. Herbes de provence rounds with sage/lavender/thyme-in-the-mix character; oregano adds italian baseline. Neither is required — bay leaf + rosemary alone is the current preferred pick. Fennel seeds (crushed in a mortar) or fennel powder add a ratatouille-adjacent lean if you want it — optional.

Don't reach for basil or parsley here — they're finishing herbs for other italian dishes, not simmer herbs for a stew.

=== BUTTER + FLOUR + DIJON MUSTARD — THE ENRICHMENT THAT TAKES IT FROM GENERIC TO HOME RUN ===

Adding butter (in the sauté alongside olive oil), flour (dusted onto the vegetables + mushrooms as a light roux before the stock goes in), and dijon mustard (stirred in near the end of the cook) is what elevates this from a generic okay lentil-mushroom-potato stew into a home-run dish. Without these three, the stew is fine but forgettable. With them, it reads distinctly better in a way that's hard to attribute to any single addition — they work together as an enrichment stack.

- BUTTER: adds dairy fat and rounded richness the pureed-mushroom + stock base lacks. Similar logic to french-chicken-soup's butter promotion.
- FLOUR (LIGHT ROUX): thickens the broth structurally as it simmers and integrates with the butter to build early body. Same technique as french-chicken-soup's dust-flour-before-deglazing move.
- DIJON MUSTARD: the most distinctive addition — see mustard-and-mushroom pairing note below.

=== MUSTARD-AND-MUSHROOM PAIRING (LIKELY DOING WHAT MISO-AND-MUSHROOM DOES IN LENTIL WELLINGTON) ===

Dijon mustard stirred into the finished stew is doing more than just adding a savory-tangy note. Working theory: mustard + mushroom in this stew is filling the same structural role that miso + mushroom fills in lentil-wellington. Both pairings are pushing the mushroom's earthy-umami into meat-analog territory that mushroom alone can't reach — mustard's sharp fermented depth (analogous to miso's fermented depth) plus mushroom's glutamate combine into something that reads meatier and more complete than either ingredient alone.

The pairings aren't interchangeable — miso is right for lentil-wellington's dense baked-log context; dijon is right for a saucy stew context — but the underlying pattern (fermented condiment + mushroom = enhanced meat-analog umami) is the same.

This is the kind of pairing worth remembering across recipes: when a mushroom-forward dish reads flat, reach for whatever fermented condiment fits the register (miso, dijon, worcestershire, tamarind) and try that as the missing structural link.

=== WINE — WALKED BACK FROM CLASHING (RE-DIAGNOSED) ===

White wine's history in this recipe: primary → removed and marked clashing ('doesn't do much; the dense base absorbs it') → NOW RE-DIAGNOSED. The earlier failures were probably not the wine's fault: either TOO MUCH WINE went in, or there wasn't enough STARCH / FLOUR / POTATOES / BUTTER in the batch to balance it. The flour + butter + wine trio balances itself — the roux-fat carries and rounds the wine's acid — and the earlier no-wine conclusion likely came from batches where that balance was off.

Wine is part of the general BALANCER TRIO for the hearty-lentil family — WINE / CREAM / MUSTARD — shared with [[milk-stout-cottage-lentils]] (where white wine was confirmed working in its second cook, alongside the already-confirmed dijon here). None of the three is a headline flavor; they round and balance without being individually tasteable.

Going forward: white wine is back as a legitimate secondary — modest amount, and make sure the enrichment stack (butter + flour roux, potatoes) is actually present to balance it.

=== NO OLD BAY, NO CANNED TOMATOES (THYME WALKED BACK FROM CLASHING) ===

- THYME: walked back from clashing — it's fine here (secondary). The bay leaf + rosemary mix remains the preferred backbone, and herbes de provence already carries some thyme in its blend, but standalone thyme doesn't hurt the dish the way the old note claimed.
- OLD BAY: belongs in italian-minestrone-soup-shaped dishes that explicitly choose it. This dish has its own herb backbone; old bay would fight it.
- CANNED TOMATOES: push the dish toward a wrong tomato register. Use fresh tomatoes (finely chopped) plus optional tomato paste — canned reads too soupy and washed-out here.

=== STOCK PREFERRED — BOUILLON SECONDARY/OKAY ===

Real stock is the preferable liquid — the mushroom-and-lentil profile benefits from stock's gentler, more layered body. But BOUILLON IS OKAY as the fallback (softened from an earlier not-bouillon stance): dissolve with a lighter hand than the package says, since cubes run concentrated and salty, and taste before adding salt anywhere else. Vegetable stock is the reliable default; beef or chicken stock work but change the register.

=== STARCH SLURRY FINISH — OPTIONAL ===

If the broth ends up thinner than you want, stir in a small starch slurry at the end. Not always needed — the pureed mushrooms, potatoes, and lentils usually carry enough body — but it's the right move when the stew is too brothy.

=== WANT TO TRY — RUTABAGA SWAP FOR CARROTS (HEARTIER, MORE MEAT-SUBSTITUTE ROLE) ===

Idea from the milk-stout-cottage-lentils work: swap carrots out of the soffrito for RUTABAGA (swede) as a heartier substitute. The reasoning connects to the 'root vegetables are the best vegetarian meat substitute' pattern documented in [[milk-stout-cottage-lentils]]'s LESSONS CONFIRMED — rutabaga at chunky-cut size does more of the meat-slot work than carrots do (carrots are sweeter/lighter and add color more than body). In this stew where the pureed mushrooms + potatoes are already carrying the meat slot, rutabaga in the soffrito would extend and reinforce that role rather than dilute it with carrot sweetness.

Untested here. Would probably want the rutabaga cut smaller than the potatoes (since it stays denser through the cook) and added at the soffrito stage rather than with the potatoes + lentils.

=== IDENTITY — WHAT MAKES THIS DISTINCT FROM [[milk-stout-cottage-lentils]] ===

The two hearty-lentil recipes share a lot of DNA (lentils, the wine/cream/mustard balancer trio, fermented-condiment depth, root vegetables) — close enough that their identities need explicit marking:

THIS RECIPE (THE STEW) is defined by:
- CELERY (the stalk, in the soffrito)
- HEAVIER TOMATO (tomato paste cooked hard as a real presence in the base)
- POTATO (finely chopped, dissolving into the broth as structural body)

[[milk-stout-cottage-lentils]] is defined by:
- DRIED SPICES (cumin seeds)
- TURNIPS / RUTABAGA (swede) as the meat slot
- CELERY ROOT (celeriac — the root, not the stalk)

Rule of thumb: stalk celery + tomato + potato-thickened broth = this stew; roots + dried spice + mash top = the cottage pie. If an experiment starts pulling one recipe toward the other's identity markers, that's the signal to stop.

=== SIBLING RECIPES ===

- lentil-wellington: same lentil + mushroom umami DNA, but in a baked-log format wrapped in puff pastry. If you like the flavor of this stew but want a fancier presentation, that's the destination.
- italian-minestrone-soup: the committed-italian-tomato-path cousin. Different structural logic (broth-forward, more vegetables); reach for that when you want a proper italian minestrone rather than the flexible stew here.
- french-chicken-soup: the committed-french-wine-and-herb-path cousin (with chicken as the protein). Different protein, different broth register.
